summary: Describes common, version-independent engineering details for the Identifier-Locator Network Protocol (ILNP), an experimental, evolutionary enhancement to IP. It comes from the IRTF Routing Research Group and defines an Experimental Protocol.

eli5.summary: This is the builder's handbook for ILNP, an experiment that separates a computer's name from its address. It tells engineers the practical details they need.

questions: how are identifiers and locators encoded in ipv6 and ipv4 packets
what dns record types does ilnp introduce
how do icmp locator updates signal connectivity changes
subtitle: Practical implementation details for identity-locator separation.

tldr.problem: ILNP architecture solves identity-location confusion, but deploying it requires defining how Identifiers and Locators fit into existing packet formats, how DNS is used, how transport protocols adapt, and how incremental deployment works.
tldr.mechanism: For ILNPv6, Identifiers and Locators fit directly into the 128-bit IPv6 address space with no router changes. For ILNPv4, Locators fit in the address field and Identifiers use IPv4 options. TCP and UDP checksums include only Identifiers, not Locators. New DNS record types (NID, L64, L32, LP) advertise Identifiers and Locators. ICMP Locator Update messages signal topology changes.
tldr.outcome: End-systems can be upgraded to support ILNP without requiring changes to router software, while maintaining compatibility with legacy IP nodes.

today: RFC 6741 is an Experimental specification from the IRTF that details how ILNP would be engineered and deployed. As with other ILNP RFCs, it remains in the research domain and has not been standardized for production use. It serves as a reference implementation guide for researchers and developers exploring identity-locator separation, but has not been widely adopted in operational networks.

sections.title: Bridging Architecture and Implementation
sections.content:
RFC 6740 describes ILNP architecture and concepts; RFC 6741 provides the engineering and implementation details that developers need to build ILNP systems. It covers aspects common to both ILNPv4 and ILNPv6—DNS, transport protocols, security, and deployment strategy—while deferring version-specific details to other RFCs.

The core engineering challenge is that only end-systems need ILNP changes; routers do not. For ILNPv6, the Identifier and Locator fit into existing IPv6 address bits, so core routers forward ILNP packets as if they were standard IPv6. For ILNPv4, Locators use the address field and Identifiers use IPv4 options, requiring ARP enhancements on edge routers but not on backbone routers.

This document defines how applications use DNS to discover ILNP support, how transport-layer protocols adapt their checksum calculations, and what new ICMP messages are needed to signal Locator changes.
sections.eli5: RFC 6740 is the blueprint; this document is the builder's manual. It explains how to encode the name and address in real packets, how to use DNS to find them, and how to tell friends your address changed.

sections.title: Packet Format: ILNPv6 and ILNPv4
sections.content:
For ILNPv6, the encoding is clean. The 128-bit IPv6 address field remains unchanged in packet format. The upper 64 bits are the Locator (syntactically identical to an IPv6 routing prefix), and the lower 64 bits are the Identifier (syntactically identical to an IPv6 interface identifier, but with different semantics). Routers forward ILNPv6 packets using the Locator (top 64 bits) with normal longest-prefix matching. ILNPv6 nodes interpret the lower 64 bits as the Identifier. IPv6 Neighbor Discovery works unmodified because it operates on the full address, which includes both Locator and Identifier.

For ILNPv4, the situation is more constrained. The 32-bit address field carries the Locator (at most 30 bits, since at least 2 bits must remain for host addressing). The 64-bit Identifier cannot fit in the address field, so it is carried in an IPv4 option header (RFC 6746). This means ILNPv4 requires ARP to be enhanced to carry Identifier information, and edge routers must recognize and forward the option header. Backbone routers treat ILNPv4 packets as ordinary IPv4 and use the address field (Locator) for forwarding.

Both versions maintain packet-format compatibility with legacy IP: an ILNPv6 packet is indistinguishable from an IPv6 packet to a router, and an ILNPv4 packet differs only by the presence of optional headers that legacy routers will forward without understanding.
sections.eli5: For IPv6, the name and address both fit in the standard address, so routers do not notice anything different. For IPv4, the address carries the location and an optional label carries the name, which old computers still forward correctly.

sections.title: DNS, Locator Updates, and Session State
sections.content:
Applications use DNS to discover ILNP support. When a node resolves a domain name, it looks for new DNS record types: NID records (store the Identifier), L64 records (IPv6 Locator), L32 records (IPv4 Locator), and LP records (pointer to Locator records, for optimization in mobile networks). If found, the application learns the peer's Identifier and one or more Locators and caches them in the ILNP Communication Cache (ILCC) with their DNS TTL values.

When a node's Locators change (due to mobility or multihoming), it sends an ICMP Locator Update message to all active correspondent nodes, listing the new set of valid Locators. This message is authenticated using an ILNP Nonce value established at session start, preventing off-path attacks. Additionally, if the node expects incoming connections, it updates its DNS records using Secure Dynamic DNS Update to register the new Locators.

Transport-layer protocols (TCP, UDP, SCTP) adapt by using only the Identifier in their session state and checksum calculations. The checksum computation includes the Identifier but zeros out the Locator fields. This allows the Locator to change in flight without breaking the checksum—a transport-layer session survives a Locator change because the Identifier remains fixed.
sections.eli5: You ask DNS: who is this person? DNS says: their name is X, and they are at address Y and Z. You write down both. When they move to address W, they send a postcard saying I am at W now. You update your records. Since you remember their name, not their address, your conversation continues.

sections.title: Backward Compatibility and Transition
sections.content:
ILNP is designed for incremental deployment. During transition, ILNP-capable nodes advertise both classic IP address records and ILNP-specific records in DNS. Old applications and systems looking up a domain find the classic A or AAAA records and work as before. New ILNP-capable applications find NID and Locator records and use them if available, falling back to the classic records if not.

An ILNP node attempting to establish a session with a peer queries DNS. If it finds ILNP records, the node includes an ILNP Nonce Option in its initial packets to signal ILNP capability. If the peer is ILNP-capable, it recognizes the Nonce and proceeds with ILNP. If the peer is not ILNP-capable, it drops the packet containing the unknown option and returns an ICMP error; the ILNP node then retries using classic IP.

A key design choice is that no router or network infrastructure changes are needed for ILNPv6 (and minimal, localized ARP changes for ILNPv4). This allows operators to deploy ILNP-capable end-systems incrementally without coordinating with network administrators or waiting for router software updates, greatly easing the deployment burden compared to previous proposals that required changes to the Internet backbone.
sections.eli5: Old computers keep using the old address records. New computers look for new records and use them if they find them, but fall back to the old records if the other computer does not understand. Nobody needs to upgrade their routers.

sections.title: Security and ILNP Nonces
sections.content:
A critical security addition is the ILNP Nonce—an unpredictable value carried in initial packets of an ILNP session. The Nonce serves two purposes. First, it prevents off-path attackers from forging ICMP Locator Update messages; without knowing the correct Nonce value, an attacker cannot convince a node to change its Locator. Second, the Nonce helps stateful firewalls authenticate ILNP control messages: the firewall can snoop the Nonce in initial packets and verify it in subsequent control messages, filtering forged messages without requiring expensive IPsec processing.

For IPsec deployments, ILNP simplifies security. Because IPsec Security Associations bind to Identifiers (not Locators), a mobile or multihomed node can change Locators without disrupting IPsec security. Traditional IPsec binds to addresses, which breaks during mobility; ILNP-aware IPsec uses Identifiers instead.

Source address filtering and other ingress filtering techniques remain effective. Because Locators have routing semantics, packets with forged Locators can be filtered using standard routing-based filters. Forged Identifiers are harder to detect but are mitigated by the ILCC cache (which records which Identifiers are valid from each peer) and by cryptographic generation of Identifiers (RFC 3972 methods).
sections.eli5: Every conversation has a secret handshake token that only the two people know. An attacker cannot hijack the conversation without the token. Because your name does not change when you move, security stays solid even as your address changes.
